title: Concert ticket drop
brief: Tickets for a huge tour go on sale at 10:00 sharp. Hundreds of thousands of fans arrive in the same minute, bots arrive earlier, and everyone refreshes when the page stalls. There are 40,000 seats. Sell each one once, charge each buyer once, and keep the site standing.

clarify.q: Is it fine to make fans wait in line?
clarify.a: Yes. A fair waiting room is much better than a broken site. Fans wait if they are told their place.

clarify.q: Can a seat be sold twice?
clarify.a: Never. A seat is held for one buyer for 5 minutes, then sold or released.

clarify.q: What about people who press refresh?
clarify.a: Many will. Every refresh can add load, and a failing payment may be retried several times by the app.

clarify.q: Can some requests be turned away?
clarify.a: A small share, yes, if bots and extra refreshes are the ones turned away. 99 percent of real people should be served.

notes: The normal day is flat at about 600 requests a second. At 10:00 sharp, traffic jumps to about 25 times that for 15 minutes (approx.).
At the top of the rush that is about 8,500 page views, 3,600 seat holds and 750 payments a second.
One database primary handles about 2,000 writes a second; payments are limited by the card company to about 1,000 a second.

hints: The site does not have to serve everyone at once. What could hold people in a fair line and let them in at a pace your database can handle?

A queue in front of the seat holds is a waiting room. A CDN serves the event page and the waiting-room page itself, and a rate limiter stops bots from taking every slot. Ticket alerts need a push service.

CDN for pages, rate limiter at the door, a queue into about 16 workers and sharded SQL (4 shards) for seat holds, about 30 servers pre-warmed because scale-up is too slow for a 30 second ramp, an idempotency store for payments, and workers sending alerts through a push service.

editorial.summary: You cannot buy your way out of a 25 times jump that lasts 15 minutes. You shape the traffic instead: serve static pages from the edge, turn away bots, queue seat holds and process them at the speed your database can take. Everyone is served in order, and nobody gets double charged.

designs.name: Waiting room in front of the seat database
designs.why: The CDN absorbs most page views. The rate limiter caps each client so bots cannot take every slot. Seat holds enter a first-in-first-out queue and workers apply them at a pace the sharded database can handle. Payments go through the idempotency store, so a retry after a timeout is never a second charge.

designs.name: Over-provisioned, no waiting room
designs.why: Skip the queue and buy enough servers and shards to take the whole rush straight through. It is simple, and the cost is a large fixed bill all month for fifteen minutes of use, with no protection if the crowd is bigger than you planned.

tradeoffs: A waiting room feels slow to a fan and stops the site from falling over. Most fans prefer a place in line to an error page.
A rate limiter set to fail closed turns people away if it breaks. Fail open lets bots through. For a sale, closed is usually the safer choice.
Pre-warmed servers cost money all month. Autoscaling cannot add servers in the 30 seconds before the first wave arrives.
First-in-first-out ordering is fair and slower than an unordered queue. For a seat sale, fairness is the point.
Retries with jitter spread repeat requests out. Without them a short blip becomes a four times bigger one.
editorial.realWorld: Big ticket sales have drawn millions of fans for tens of thousands of seats, and large sellers now use queues or timed access to control the rate (approx.).

correctness.prompt: A 5-minute seat hold expires as payment succeeds. What seat schema and state transitions prevent two buyers from owning the seat?
correctness.discussion: Keep one authoritative row per flight or event and seat, with owner, hold token, expires_at and state. Acquire a 5-minute hold with an atomic conditional update. Move available to held to sold only if the buyer's token still owns an unexpired hold; the expiry worker must check that same token and state before releasing it. Enforce one sale per seat with a unique constraint. Charge using a stable payment idempotency key and reconcile unknown outcomes. If payment succeeds after the hold was lost, refund or void it instead of selling the seat again. Sync replication and a queue do not supply these transaction rules.

fields.label: Seat hold transaction
options: Read availability, then write a hold
Conditionally claim the seat in one transaction
fields.explanation: Claim the authoritative seat atomically and bind it to an owner, hold token and expiry. Expiry and sale must check that same token and state.

fields.label: Payment timeout
options: Keep payment pending and reconcile with the same key
Mark it failed and charge with a fresh key
fields.explanation: A timeout leaves payment pending with an unknown outcome. Reconcile it using the same key. Confirm the sale only for a valid hold; refund or void a late success after the hold is lost. Terminal success must not be overwritten by a late failure.

correctness.limits: The traffic score does not verify exclusive seat ownership, atomic hold expiry, payment state transitions or refunds after a lost hold.
